location.value: The northern tip of Sumatra, at the entrance to the Strait of Malacca. At its peak it controlled most of Sumatra’s coasts and parts of the Malay Peninsula (Pahang, Kedah).

terrain.value: Coastal plains with mountainous interior. The capital Kutaraja (Banda Aceh) faced the Bay of Bengal trade routes.

climate.value: Tropical and wet, suited to pepper.

resources.value: Pepper, plus gold, tin (after taking Pahang in 1617), betel nuts and spices. In the 1820s Aceh produced over half the world’s pepper.

disasters.value: No specific disasters are recorded for the sultanate in the sources checked. The region was devastated by the 2004 tsunami, long after the sultanate ended.

population.value: No population figure is given in the sources checked.

urbanisation.value: Banda Aceh was a major port city and Islamic centre, known as the “porch of Mecca” (Serambi Mekkah).

disease.value: The sultan died of cholera in the hills after the Dutch captured the palace in 1874.

migration.value: Pilgrims and scholars travelled between Aceh and Mecca. Hostages and captives were brought from conquered states.

economicBase.value: Pepper exports and control of trade at the northern end of the Strait of Malacca.

tradeRoutes.value: Pepper and gold to Gujarat, the Ottoman Red Sea, China, and later English and Dutch companies. It competed with Portuguese Malacca and Johor.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold and silver coins (dirham/deureuham), plus kupang and keueh coins. Its gold currency was a source of strength, but the food supply was fragile.

inequality.value: Power shifted from the sultan to regional chiefs (uleebalang) and wealthy “pepper rajas”.

governmentType.value: A centralised absolute monarchy (c. 1496–1641). Then rule by queens (1641–1699). Then a decentralised sultanate dominated by uleebalang chiefs (1699–1873). Then a wartime monarchy until 1903.

keyRulers.value: Ali Mughayat Syah (c. 1514–1530, unifier). Alauddin al-Kahar (c. 1539–1571). Iskandar Muda (1607–1636, peak). Sultanah Safiatuddin (1641–1675, first of four queens). Muhammad Daud Syah II (1875–1903, last).

succession.value: Hereditary, unusually including four female rulers in a row (1641–1699). Later disputes led to a civil war (1814–1819).

institutions.value: Iskandar Muda’s code (Adat Meukuta Alam). Districts (mukim) headed by uleebalang. Rotating governors. Islamic law and scholars at court.

stability.value: Strong central rule under Iskandar Muda, then gradual decentralisation, a succession crisis (1764–73) and civil war (1814–19).

eliteConflict.value: Iskandar Muda removed or replaced the old nobility. Later the uleebalang and religious leaders competed with the sultan.

armyAndTech.value: Large fleets and armies with cannon. Ottoman gunners and a relief fleet (from the 1560s) helped. It lost 19,000 men and its fleet at Malacca in 1629, according to a Portuguese account.

majorWars.value: Conflicts with Portugal (1519–1639, including sieges of Malacca in 1568 and 1629). Conquests of Pahang (1617) and Kedah (1619). The Aceh War against the Netherlands (1873–1904/1914).

territoryChange.value: Expanded across Sumatra and the peninsula under Iskandar Muda. Shrank after 1629. Annexed by the Dutch, a long process from 1874 to 1904.

alliancesRivals.value: Ally: the Ottoman Empire, which it claimed as protector from 1569. Rivals: Portugal, Johor, and later the Netherlands.

inventions.value: Cannon casting with Ottoman help, and fortifications.

scienceEducation.value: A major centre of Islamic scholarship (Hamzah Fansuri, Syamsuddin of Pasai, Nuruddin ar-Raniri, Abdurrauf of Singkil). Religious texts were translated into Malay.

openness.value: Open to Ottoman, Indian and Arab ties and to English trade (James Lancaster, 1602). Hostile to Portugal and later the Dutch.

religion.value: Sunni Islam, with strong scholarly and Sufi traditions.

languageWriting.value: Acehnese, Malay and Arabic, written in Jawi script.

artsArchitecture.value: The Hikayat Aceh chronicle and the Hikayat Prang Sabi (“Tale of the Holy War”) poems. Royal tomb complexes and the Baiturrahman mosque tradition in Banda Aceh.

socialStructure.value: Sultan, uleebalang chiefs, ulama (religious scholars), merchants, commoners, and slaves (an 1873 illustration shows a slave market).

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Islamic and Acehnese identity, which sustained decades of resistance to the Dutch and remains strong today.

neighbours.value: Portuguese and later Dutch Malacca, Johor, Pahang, Kedah, Pedir, Pasai, Deli, and the Ottoman Empire.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Islam and Islamic scholarship across the Malay world. Dutch (Cornelis de Houtman, 1599) and English (Lancaster, 1602) visitors arrived early.

colonisation.value: Colonised: the Dutch captured the capital in 1874 and dissolved the sultanate (1903/1904), though resistance continued for years.

riseSignals.value: Ali Mughayat Syah united the northern Sumatran ports (c. 1514–1530). After the Portuguese took Malacca (1511), Muslim traders moved to Aceh. Pepper wealth and Ottoman support followed.

declineSignals.value: The 1629 disaster at Malacca, the Dutch capture of Malacca (1641) and the VOC’s control of trade, decentralisation of power, and civil wars.

outcome.value: Conquest. The Aceh War (from 1873) ended with the sultan’s surrender in 1903 and the dissolution of the sultanate (1904). Guerrilla resistance continued until about 1912–1914.

sources.value: Malay chronicles (Hikayat Aceh), Portuguese, Dutch, English and Ottoman records. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Ricklefs (2008).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. The founding date varies (1480, 1496 or c. 1514–1520) and the end date varies (1903, 1904, or 1912–14 counting resistance). Some figures come only from Portuguese accounts.
